beats.narration_text: Read "Claude issues legal holds" and the natural inference is that Claude is the one making the call — deciding, on its own, when a lawsuit means the documents get frozen.

Here's what actually happens. Before issuing or releasing anything, the skill stops and asks: have you cleared this with an attorney? Answer no, and instead of firing off a notice, it hands you a one-page brief to walk into their office with. The stop is the whole design choice.

What is a skill, mechanically? One file. Legal-hold is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — plain English, no code — telling Claude how to draft the hold notice, log the case fields, and calendar the next refresh. Text you can read is text you can audit; that's the design bet.

The routing is literal. You pass a flag — issue, refresh, release, or status — and the file runs the steps for that one mode, in order: capture the details, draft the document, update the log. No branching to hide in.

The spec also draws its own edges. It drafts, it logs, it calendars — it does not enforce preservation, does not set scope on its own, and does not send the notice. A person does every one of those. Trade-off: no autonomy, but no runaway either.

So the file never taught Claude when a lawsuit calls for a hold — that judgment stays with the person. What it guarantees is that once a person says issue, refresh, or release, Claude reads that same SKILL.md and produces the same notice, the same log update, the same next date. Repeatability, not judgment.

beats.narration_text: Two directions of misreading. A clean, on-time notice doesn't prove Claude understood the lawsuit — a checklist can be followed to the letter on a case it never grasped. And a stall doesn't prove the skill is broken — the written steps may simply not cover what was asked. The output is evidence of the file, not the case.
A legal-hold skill doesn't hand Claude legal judgment. It hands it a file that drafts the notice — and then waits for a person to say yes.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want a SKILL.md for something I do the same way every time — a checklist my future self, or a colleague, can follow without me being in the room. Here's the process, in plain language — paste it in. Turn it into a SKILL.md with these pieces: one line saying when to invoke it; the ordered steps; the specific information the person needs to gather before starting; the ways it can fail and how to notice; and critically, anything the skill must not do without an explicit human yes. Read the finished file back to me and walk me through exactly what you'd do if I ran it, before you do anything. Go deeper: ask the same model to name three points in your process where a human yes should be required — and why the cost of a wrong autonomous action at each point outweighs the friction of asking.
